Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Patrick would be ~35 in 1880. Crucially, the 1880 census is the first to record each person's stated relationship to the head of household — if Patrick is enumerated in Thomas's household (Thomas ~62), the enumerator would record 'son,' which is stronger evidence than mere co-enumeration in earlier years. If Patrick has his own household by then, Thomas may appear as a boarder or parent, again with a stated relationship. The collection 'United States Census, 1880' (1417683) is name-searchable.

Patrick died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County. Pennsylvania civil death registration began in 1906, so a state death certificate exists. S3 ('Pennsylvania Death Certificates') is already cited in the tree for Patrick's death fact, but no assertions naming his parents have been extracted from it for q_001. The informant (typically a family member) may have provided Patrick's father's name, mother's maiden name, and birthplace — all primary parentage evidence. The birth-parish discrepancy (tree records Ireland; objective says Pennsylvania) may also be resolved here.

A will filed by Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage. The loc_001 locality entry notes that probate records are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811 and are available via FamilySearch. The collection 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), so this requires an image browse of the county probate dockets rather than a name search. Thomas was born ~1818; his death is unknown but could plausibly fall anywhere from ~1858 to ~1910, so the item's date range is set to Thomas's plausible death window rather than Patrick's research window.

A dedicated search for the marriage record of Thomas Flynn and his wife is required for a parentage question. This record (a) confirms the couple as a unit; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which no census or the 1908 death certificate is likely to give; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845), corroborates that Thomas was the father of a child named on later derivative sources such as a death certificate or single co-residence. Note the limit: the marriage record alone does not prove Patrick is their child — it establishes the couple and dates their union. loc_001 notes that Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia through this period; the collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. The mother's surname produced here should be treated as her surname at time of this marriage, which may be a prior married name rather than her birth name; a companion search for her earlier marriages or her own baptism may be needed if remarriage is suspected.

If Patrick was born in Schuylkill County (as the objective states, in contrast to Ireland in the tree), a Catholic baptism record would directly name his parents and constitute primary evidence of parentage. The collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. If the baptism cannot be found — because Patrick was born in Ireland as the tree records, or because the parish register predates surviving records — the absence shifts the search toward his death certificate (pli_008) and the 1880 census (pli_007) as the route to an origin, in keeping with loc_001's note that pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate rather than civil records.

FAN cluster item. If Thomas Flynn had other children, their baptism entries in Schuylkill County Catholic registers would each name Thomas and his wife as parents — directly confirming the family unit and identifying the mother. A sibling's baptism is stronger than co-enumeration alone because it places the same parental pair with a named child in a primary record. The collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. Search for Flynn children baptized in the county across the range when Thomas (born ~1818) would have been raising a family; any match becomes a sibling lead and a corroborating parentage source for Patrick.

**Plan pl_002 — 10 items (pli_004 through pli_013):**

- **pli_004** — vital_record, Schuylkill County, 1908, FamilySearch: Patrick's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate; name-searchable; S3 is already in the tree on the relationship but no parentage assertions have been extracted — this is the highest-probability direct evidence source (death certs of this era name father and mother). - **pli_008** — census, Schuylkill County, 1900, FamilySearch: 1900 US Census (collection 1325221), name-searchable; lists month/year of birth, years married, and each person's parents' birthplaces — corroborates Ireland as Patrick's (and his parents') origin.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

The Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317) is name-searchable and covers exactly this date. Death certificates of this era name the informant's statement of the deceased's father and mother, making this the highest-probability record for direct parentage evidence. The tree cites S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates) on Patrick's death fact (F2) and on the ParentChild relationship (R1), but no assertions from that certificate have been extracted for this question. Patrick would be approximately 15 in 1860 and likely still in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County. The United States Census, 1860 (collection 1473181) is name-searchable. The tree already cites S2 (1860 U.S. Federal Census) on the ParentChild relationship (R1) between Thomas (I2) and Patrick (I1), but no assertions from that record have been extracted for this question. Finding Patrick enumerated in Thomas's household in both 1850 and 1860 would substantially strengthen the household-membership corroboration of the parentage hypothesis. The 1880 federal census is the first to name each person's relationship to the head of household explicitly. Patrick would be approximately 35; Thomas would be approximately 62 and may still be alive. The United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable. If Patrick and Thomas are co-resident in 1880, the relationship field is direct evidence of parentage; if in separate but proximate households, their enumeration districts guide the probate-volume browse in item pli_010. If the FamilySearch search (pli_006) does not locate Patrick or Thomas Flynn under any variant, Ancestry's census collection is the cross-check, following the same two-repository approach used for the 1850 census in the completed plan for q_002 (pl_001). A marriage record for Thomas Flynn and his wife (Patrick's mother) would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's maiden name which no existing source records, and by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845) corroborate Thomas as a parent otherwise evidenced only by household co-enumeration. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Searching Patrick in the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses will establish when Patrick himself moved, what occupation he held, and whether he and Michael later shared a neighborhood or household. Patrick's migration trajectory reveals the family network that Michael plausibly followed.

Pennsylvania's Bureau of Mines (established 1870) published annual reports naming individual collieries, their operators, and sometimes employees. For a subject tree records as 'Miner' in Schuylkill County from 1882 (fact F3, unsourced), these mine inspector annual reports for 1882-1895 are the occupation-specific government record that could confirm his mining employment, identify his employer or colliery, and document the economic conditions drawing labor to the region. Reports are held by the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg; digitized copies are available through HathiTrust and the Internet Archive.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

It then moves to records that could name his specific employer: Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines annual inspection reports, which listed collieries and sometimes individual workers. The church records collection for Schuylkill County could date his arrival at a local Catholic parish and sometimes name the parish he transferred from. The county's naturalization records (images to be browsed page by page) may show when he settled in the county and what occupation he declared. Finally, the Miners' Journal — the principal newspaper of the anthracite coal region — is searched in its digitized form for accident reports, union filings, or employment notices bearing his name.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) would be ~25 in 1870 — an adult, likely forming his own household or boarding. The United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Though the 1870 schedule does not record each person's relationship to the head of household (that column was not introduced until 1880), finding Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, now ~52) enumerated in the same household as Patrick would add a third decade of co-residence evidence to the two already established in 1850 and 1860, further strengthening the parentage inference. The search should also try variant spellings such as Flyn and Flinn.

If Thomas Flynn does not appear in Patrick's 1870 household, search for Thomas Flynn directly in Schuylkill County. Thomas (born ~1818) would be ~52 and plausibly still alive and resident in the county. Finding Thomas in his own household — particularly with other members sharing the Flynn surname — would provide context for the family's composition after Patrick reached adulthood, and any member named Patrick would be direct corroboration of the relationship.

The 1880 census is the most probative of the three for this question because it was the first federal census to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. Patrick (~35) is old enough to be a household head; if Thomas Flynn appears in Patrick's 1880 household listed as 'Father,' that is direct parentage evidence on an original government record — far stronger than the inferred co-residence evidence from 1850 and 1860. Thomas (born ~1818) would be ~62 in 1880 and plausibly still alive. The United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable.

If Thomas is not in Patrick's 1880 household, search for Thomas Flynn directly. The 1880 relationship column in his own household would list any children still at home, and a Patrick Flynn listed as 'Son' to Thomas would constitute direct parentage evidence. The 1880 schedule also records each person's birthplace and their parents' birthplaces, which could confirm the family's Irish origin and further corroborate the parentage conclusion.

Patrick Flynn (d. 1908) will appear in the 1900 census at approximately age 55. The 1900 schedule is uniquely valuable because it asks for each person's parents' birthplaces, which could confirm Thomas Flynn's origin in Ireland — corroborating the parentage conclusion independently of the 1908 death certificate's secondary informant. The 1900 schedule also records years in the United States and citizenship status, which may help date the family's immigration. The United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable. Note: the 1890 census was largely destroyed by fire in 1921 and cannot fill the gap between 1880 and 1900.

The 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father but was reported by a secondary informant (son-in-law James Brown). Finding Thomas Flynn's will naming Patrick as a son would provide direct parentage evidence on an original legal document and would advance the conclusion from 'probable' to 'proved.' The date range 1861-1900 covers Thomas's plausible death years: he was confirmed alive in 1860 and born ~1818, so he plausibly died between 1861 and roughly 1900 (at ~82); the census items above may help narrow this window. The loc_001 locality entry confirms Schuylkill County probate records (wills and administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills and are available from 1811. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) on FamilySearch is browse-only (personCount 0) — search by browsing the Schuylkill County volume by year rather than by name.

- Patrick Flynn (I1): birth ~1845 Ireland (from 1850 and 1860 census co-residence), death 1908-03-12 Schuylkill County, PA (from death certificate S3)

- **pli_008** — census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1880, FamilySearch: The United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable and is the most probative year — the first census to record explicit relationships. Thomas (~62) listed as "Father" in Patrick's household would be direct parentage evidence on an original government record.
- **pli_009** — census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1880, FamilySearch (fallback for pli_008): If Thomas is not in Patrick's 1880 household, search for Thomas directly; a "Son" named Patrick in Thomas's household is direct evidence; the 1880 parental birthplace fields would also confirm Irish origin.
- **pli_010** — census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1900, FamilySearch: The United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable. **Total scope:** six searches (five name searches, one image browse).

**Fallback relationships:** pli_007 runs only if Thomas is absent from pli_006's result; pli_009 runs only if Thomas is absent from pli_008's result.

**Hand-back:** search-records for pli_006, pli_007, pli_008, pli_009, and pli_010 (all FamilySearch name-searchable collections); search-records also for pli_011 (FamilySearch browse of Pennsylvania Probate Records, collection 1999196). The delegation did not authorize immediate execution.

The existing evidence — Patrick appearing in Thomas's household in both the 1850 and 1860 censuses, plus a 1908 death certificate naming Thomas as father — is suggestive but falls short of proved, partly because neither early census stated relationships and the death certificate came from a secondary informant. This new plan works through the three remaining federal census years to track Patrick as an adult and look for Thomas in his household: 1870 and 1880 are searched in that order, with a fallback search targeting Thomas directly if he isn't in Patrick's household, and 1880 is especially important because that was the first census to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. The 1900 census follows, valuable for its parental-birthplace fields, and the plan closes with an image browse of Schuylkill County's probate records to find whether Thomas left a will naming Patrick as his son.

The 1860 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1473181, name-searchable) would show Patrick at approximately age 15. Finding him in Thomas Flynn's household a second time—a decade after the 1850 co-enumeration (a_004)—extends the indirect co-residence evidence for the Thomas-as-father hypothesis. The project tree cites this census as S2 on the parent-child relationship, but no parentage assertions have been extracted for q_001; this search anchors those assertions directly to the parentage question. Search for both Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County, with variant spellings Flinn and Flyn.

Thomas Flynn (born ca. 1818 in Ireland) plausibly died between 1851 and ca. 1900. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), as is the Schuylkill County probate image group 007936749 (1851–1930); browse both for a Thomas Flynn will or administration. A will explicitly naming Patrick as a son is direct evidence of parentage—the strongest available source short of a baptism record. The loc_001 entry confirms the Register of Wills has held Schuylkill County probate records since 1811. The date range is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan as a father of a child born ca. 1845, not by Patrick's own research window.

If the FamilySearch digital images (pli_006) do not yield a Thomas Flynn probate file, contact the Schuylkill County Register of Wills directly for a docket search covering 1851–1900. The loc_001 entry identifies this office as the custodian of the original records. Docket books list all filings by surname and name the heirs, so a Thomas Flynn entry naming Patrick as heir would constitute direct evidence of parentage even without the full will.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife is required by the parentage question. Their marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name—which no census or death certificate typically carries—and by its date relative to Patrick's birth (ca. 1845) corroborates Thomas as the father even when no record yet explicitly places Patrick as their son. Note the limit: the couple's marriage proves they married and dates their union but does not by itself establish Patrick as their child. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985) is name-searchable. The Flynn family was likely Roman Catholic; Schuylkill County's RC parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (per loc_001), and sacramental registers were held at the parish level. Thomas born ca. 1818 would have married roughly 1838–1855; the 1842 lower bound reflects when Schuylkill County church records first appear in this collection. By 1870 Patrick may head his own household or may still live with Thomas. Searching both names tracks the evolving household structure and extends the co-residence chain from 1850 and 1860. If Thomas's household in 1870 names a wife, her given name becomes a lead for the marriage search (pli_008). An Ancestry version of this census (external collection ancestry:7163) is a paid fallback if FamilySearch returns no results.

The 1880 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1417683, name-searchable) records each person's relationship to the head of household explicitly. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
